autointerp.description: The feature fires on tokens inside the model's re-reading or quoting of the problem statement during a "Wait, let me re-check the wording" step, typically at a point where a quoted phrase or number from the problem is being copied word by word.

The feature fires on the subject noun (or key noun) of a clause in the model's step-by-step reasoning, especially after "Wait," or "if the", just before a predicate like "is" that restates or re-checks a quantity or fact from the problem.
This feature fires on a token in the middle of the model's "Wait, is it possible that…" / "If he does X…" re-examination of a problem's wording, usually on the word or phrase being reinterpreted.

This feature fires on tokens inside a repeated phrase, where the model is copying or re-quoting text it has just written or read in the prompt (often right after "Wait," or when restating the problem), so it predicts the next token from the earlier occurrence.

This feature fires on a token that begins re-quoting or re-reading a phrase from the problem statement, usually right after a "Wait, if/does/is..." self-check, where the model repeats the problem's wording to verify its interpretation.

It fires on a word or number in the model's mid-solution self-questioning ("Wait, if...") where it re-examines an interpretation, usually the key quantity or noun being questioned or emphasized, often repeating a term from the problem.

The feature fires on tokens inside a quoted or hypothesized rewording of the problem, where the model is considering that the question may have been phrased or typed differently (e.g. "maybe the question meant…") and is writing out the alternative version, especially at the point where it differs from the original.

This feature fires on a token in the model's mid-solution self-checking or re-reading passages, usually the word that starts or continues a short restatement of a problem element, where the model is verifying wording, units or a simple example.

It fires on a token in the middle of a clause that the model is repeating or restating from earlier text, typically right after "Wait, if..." or "If...", where it re-quotes the premise word by word (often just before the clause's verb or object continues).

The feature fires on tokens in the middle of the model restating or re-reading part of a problem during a "Wait, …" self-check, where it is about to copy the next element of a quoted phrase, list, or expression (e.g., "and", "+", a number, or a repeated word).

It fires on the last token of a sentence or clause in a step-by-step math solution that introduces an upcoming calculation, typically the period or final noun right before a colon or displayed equation.

The feature fires on a token in the middle of a repeated or restated phrase, typically after "Wait, if/is it…", where the model is about to copy or re-derive text it just wrote, so it predicts the next token as a repetition of the earlier one.

It fires on the newline/indentation whitespace token at the end of a line in the model's step-by-step reasoning, just before it starts a new bullet or "Wait," line that second-guesses or re-examines the previous step.

It fires on the whitespace/indentation (or bullet) token at the start of a new line in a bulleted reasoning list, immediately before the model writes "Wait," to second-guess or revise its previous step.

The feature fires on the final token of a clause in the model's self-correcting "Wait, if/what if..." reasoning, where it is restating a premise or condition and the token completes a repeated or predictable phrase (e.g., "away from [home]", "has [2]").

This feature fires on tokens inside a "Wait, ..." self-correction line where the model is repeating, nearly verbatim, text from the preceding line or its own earlier reasoning, so it's copying the next token of a phrase it just wrote.

This feature fires inside the model's reasoning when it is second-guessing a problem's wording ("Is it possible the question implies…", "Maybe it means…"), on the token in the proposed alternative reading just before the word or phrase it would reinterpret, which is often italicized.
This feature fires on the token just before a numeric result is written, typically the space or minus sign after an "=" in an arithmetic step, where the model is about to output the computed number.

The feature fires on the final token of a short phrase the model quotes verbatim from the problem statement while it re-reads and double-checks the wording, usually in a "Wait, is it possible…? No, the text says '…'" kind of passage.

The feature fires on the final word or noun-like token inside a quoted excerpt of the problem statement that the model is re-reading to check its wording, typically the object or complement at the point where the quote is cut off.

This feature fires on a function word (often "with", "or", "having", "of", "had") that comes right after a noun or noun phrase and introduces a modifier, attribute or following clause, as in "animals [with] spikes" or "identified as [having] recently left".

The feature fires on the verb or noun in the model's mid-solution musings about how to interpret a word problem's wording, where it is working out what the phrase refers to (a state, condition, event, or action) and the next token will complete that interpretive clause.

This feature fires on the word "coordinate(s)" and nearby words with a similar sense, such as "coordination," "coordinator," "ordered (pair)," "projection," and "address," which relate to specifying positions or organizing things in order, especially in geometry and math contexts.

The feature fires at the end of a quoted phrase or sentence from the problem statement (often the closing quote or punctuation) as the model is re-reading and scrutinizing the wording, right before it comments on or interprets what that quoted text means.
The feature fires on the word "such" when it begins a construction like "such that", "such as", or "such a", coming right after a noun or verb phrase.

It fires on a noun or noun-phrase token that repeats an entity or concept already mentioned earlier in the context, particularly the head noun being re-referenced (for example "bicycle," "County," "NASCAR," "cars").

It fires on a function word (often "the", "of", "for", "than", "another") right after a verb like "is/are" or a conjunction, where the model is restating or interpreting a problem's relationships and the next words will name a role or referent (e.g., "the one who...", "the sides", "the container

It fires on a mid-word fragment in a word that is split into multiple tokens, typically a single consonant or short chunk (like "p", "m", "w", "r") that begins a later syllable of a rare or compound word, such as a place name or a compound like "northwesterly" or "hed

The feature fires on the token that fills the next slot in a parallel, enumerated structure (the third item in a series, the second of a pair, the matching element in a repeated pattern), where the model is predicting continuation of that parallel list or template.

This feature fires in the opening sentence of a Wikipedia article, on the token that completes the subject's name or parenthetical (a closing parenthesis, the last word of the title, or the "was/is" that follows) just before the main predicate describing what the subject is.

The feature fires on tokens inside a phrase the model is repeating or re-reading verbatim (often after "Wait,"), where the token is a mid-copy continuation that the model can predict by matching the earlier occurrence.

This feature fires on tokens in the middle of a clause right after a self-correcting "Wait, ..." in the model's reasoning, typically the noun or verb in a hypothesis being re-examined (e.g. "is an [interruption]?", "if f [decreases]", "EN is

This feature fires on the content-bearing words (verbs, nouns) in the first sentence of the final written solution that follows the `</think>` tag, where the model begins restating how it will solve the problem.
This feature fires on tokens in a maths word problem where the model is about to copy or repeat a word, number, or phrase from earlier in the problem, so it is predicting a verbatim continuation.

The feature fires on the verb or connective right after a hypothetical "if ... / Wait, ..." clause in the model's self-checking reasoning, where it begins restating or working out the consequence of that scenario (often by repeating the preceding expression).

This feature fires on the first token or two of a math expression, just after "$", when the model is restating or re-checking an expression it already wrote (typically after "Wait," or a similar self-correction cue).

This feature fires on the token right after a "Wait," (or similar re-checking phrase) in a model's self-doubting reasoning, where it begins re-examining or repeating a previous claim, such as "if", "actually", "I think", or "possible".

The feature fires on tokens inside a phrase or expression that is being repeated or re-quoted verbatim from earlier text, especially in "Wait, ..." self-correction passages where the model copies the previous wording and the token is the next one to be copied.

The feature fires on the verb or key word in the middle of a conditional clause ("Wait, if X ...", "If he turns around") that the model writes while re-examining a problem's assumptions or interpretation in its reasoning.

This feature fires on the first token of a new line or clause that restates or re-examines a subject (a quoted phrase, a title, or an "if/wait" reconsideration), typically the opening word that begins a sentence or quoted item right after a line break or "Wait,".

This feature mostly fires on the double-newline token that ends the opening sentence of a model's thinking ("Here's my thought process...:") just before the numbered list begins, and it fires more weakly on other tokens that are highly predictable from boilerplate or memorized text.

This feature fires on tokens inside a phrase the model is repeating verbatim from an immediately preceding line, typically during a "Wait, if..." self-correction loop, where it predicts that the copied text will continue.

It fires on a word or symbol in the middle of the model's "Wait, …" self-checking passages, where it re-reads or restates part of the problem (a verb, noun, or term from the quoted phrase) just before it checks that phrase's meaning or consistency.

The feature fires on tokens in the middle of a phrase that the model is re-reading or restating while double-checking its reasoning (typically after "Wait, if..." or "Is it possible..."), where it is copying or paraphrasing earlier wording from the problem or its own earlier steps

It fires on a mid-word or mid-name token in a multi-token proper noun or technical term (such as "D|under| Mifflin", "Cal|ak|mul" or "Dir|ich|let"), where the next token is a predictable completion of a name or word the model has to finish.

The feature fires on tokens inside the consequent clause of a hypothetical "If X, (then) Y" statement in the model's step-by-step reasoning, typically at the subject or verb right after the condition, where the model is working out what follows from a scenario.

The feature fires on the subject or verb token inside a re-examined hypothetical or quoted clause (often after "Wait, if...") in a model's second-guessing of a word problem, just before the clause's predicate or object is completed.

The feature fires on tokens in the middle of a phrase the model is re-typing verbatim, copying a clause it has just written (often after "Wait," or "If") as it restates or re-examines its own earlier wording.

The feature fires on tokens in the middle of a multi-token unit where the next token is highly predictable from memorized or formulaic context, such as partial words in names and titles, the start-of-turn token, or fixed phrases like "step by step".

The feature fires on a token inside a math expression (a variable, subscript, or digit) at the point where the model is about to copy or continue a term from a pattern it has just seen, often during a "Wait" re-check.

The feature fires on tokens in the model's self-correcting "Wait, is it possible the problem meant…" passages, where it restates or re-quotes part of the problem or earlier reasoning just before an alternative reading is spelled out, typically a few tokens before an emphasized or substitu

It fires on the token right after the subject of a hypothetical "if/wait, what if" clause in the model's self-checking reasoning, where it is considering an alternative interpretation of a word problem, typically the noun or verb that follows the subject and leads into the predicate.

The feature fires on the sentence-ending punctuation (period, question mark, or closing parenthesis) that ends a clause in the model's self-doubting reasoning, typically after a "Wait, if…" or "If…" conditional restatement of a problem condition, just before it moves on to

It fires on the paragraph-break newline token that comes right after the model finishes a step-by-step computation or draft solution and just before it writes a brief verification comment such as "Looks good," "Looks solid," or "Wait, did...".

It fires on the token just before an opening quotation mark, where the model is about to quote or re-read a phrase verbatim from the problem statement (often a colon, "and", "vs", or a verb) while checking its wording.

The feature fires on structural tokens (newlines, indentation, list markers, numbering) at points in the model's reasoning where an enumerated list or parallel structure is being laid out and the next item is expected to follow the pattern of the previous ones.

The feature fires on the opening quotation mark that begins a quoted word-problem statement, typically when the model is recalling or restating a similar or alternative version of the problem in its reasoning.

The feature fires on the whitespace token after a bullet marker ("*") at the start of a new indented bullet line in a model's chain-of-thought reasoning, right where the next reasoning step (often a "Wait," "Let's check," or "Usually," re-evaluation) is about to

This feature fires on function words and punctuation (prepositions, periods, commas, "as," "versus," "by") at points where the next token is a highly predictable continuation, such as a name or a clause boundary, in encyclopedic or structured text.
The token "been" immediately following an auxiliary "has/had/having" in a perfect construction, where the model is predicting the participle or complement that comes next.

The word "If" that begins a conditional sentence in the model's reasoning, usually right after it has posed a question or alternative interpretation and is now starting to explore what follows from that hypothesis.
The feature fires on the second operand's digit in a simple arithmetic expression being computed or double-checked, at the point where the model is about to write the "=" and the result.

This feature fires on tokens in the middle of a word or expression where the model is predicting a specific continuation, often "adopt"-related words (adopt, adopted, adapting) or subtraction/exponent terms like "-k", which look like token-level pattern completions.
The feature fires on LaTeX fraction syntax tokens, specifically the "frac" in `\frac` or the `}{` junction between numerator and denominator, where the denominator is about to be written.

It fires on a word that sits mid-phrase in a financial, economic or statistical context (hospital charges, median counts, income, prosperity, success, finishes, households), where the token seems to anticipate a following noun or number.

It fires on tokens in the run-up to or within a mention of a storm or severe weather event (e.g., "gale", "hurricane", "typhoon", "torrential rain", "in the event of a"), often predicting that a weather term or event will come next.
This feature fires on formatting tokens (indentation whitespace, periods, colons, newlines) at the end of a line or step in the model's structured reasoning, right before a new line or step begins.

The feature fires on the token just before the result of an arithmetic calculation is written (the equals sign, a space, a minus sign, or the leading digit), where the model is about to output the answer's digits, often one ending in 6 or a round sum.

It fires on a token that repeats or restates a word, number, or expression from earlier in the text, typically when the model is re-checking or re-reading the problem with "Wait, if..." and copying a phrase it is about to analyze.
It fires on a mid-word or mid-name token in a multi-token proper noun (a person's name, place, or organization), where the next token must complete the name.

This feature fires on the subject or function word (often a name, "if", "has", "have", or "is") in the middle of the model's own self-questioning, "Wait, ..." re-checks of the problem wording, where it is about to restate or reconsider what the prompt says.

It fires on the opening quote mark (or the first word right after it) when the model, while double-checking, re-reads the problem and begins quoting or re-reading a specific phrase from the prompt or code.

It fires on tokens inside a conditional "if…" clause in the model's mid-solution self-questioning (often after "Wait,"), where it is re-examining an assumption or interpretation of the problem and the clause's condition is still being spelled out.

It fires on tokens in the middle of a hedging "Wait, if…" or "If…" restatement in the model's self-correcting reasoning, where it re-examines a conditional premise of the problem and is partway through repeating a clause it has already considered.

It fires on sentence- or clause-ending tokens (periods, closing parentheses, colons, bold markers) in step-by-step math solutions, right after a given fact or setup has been stated and just before the model moves on to the next calculation or relationship.

The feature fires on tokens inside a sentence the model is repeating verbatim from a line just before it (typically after "Wait," in a self-correcting reasoning loop), as it copies the earlier phrase word by word.
